pages.title: UAIS
pages.subtitle: Universal AI Safety Architecture
pages.kicker: English short visual edition · Draft 1.0 Candidate 3 · Public Review
pages.lead: A constitutional architecture for a world where AI capability grows faster than ordinary rules, but consequential authority must remain explicitly granted, bounded, observable, and revocable.

notes.title: Core shift
notes.body: Can do ≠ may do.

notes.title: Public Review
notes.body: Public Review means Candidate 3 is open for external critique. It does not mean the architecture has been independently validated, adopted, certified, or endorsed.

notes.title: Status
notes.body: This is not an adopted standard, a certification scheme, or a guarantee of AI safety.

pages.title: Contents
pages.subtitle: Twenty visual sheets
pages.lead: Each sheet explains one architectural idea and links back to the source sections of the public Candidate 3 specification.

pages.title: What is UAIS?
pages.subtitle: Not control of intelligence; control of unaccountable power
pages.lead: UAIS separates what a system can do from what it is allowed to do. As AI becomes more capable, access to money, devices, production, accounts, and other consequential interfaces must stay explicitly granted, bounded, and revocable.

notes.title: Same consequence, same boundary
notes.body: If the consequence is the same, the protected boundary should apply to a human, script, AI system, robot, service, or coordinated group.

notes.title: Not actor-blind
notes.body: Authorization may still depend on identity, role, authentication, purpose, context, demonstrated trustworthiness, and legitimate mandate.

notes.title: Bottom line
notes.body: UAIS does not limit intelligence. It limits unaccountable power.

pages.title: How UAIS emerged
pages.subtitle: From AI capability to a constitution of authority
pages.lead: The old question, “is the model safe?”, became too narrow once AI systems gained tools, memory, networks, agents, and physical interfaces. Answers became actions; actions became consequences.

notes.title: 1 · Capability grew
notes.body: We learned to measure what a system can do, but not who gave it the right to launch the resulting consequences.

notes.title: 2 · The old question broke
notes.body: “Safe model” does not say who grants authority, where it ends, or who can revoke it.

notes.title: Can do ≠ may do
notes.body: The ability to perform an action does not create authority.

notes.title: 3 · Authority needed structure
notes.body: The architecture must show who grants authority, where the boundary lies, what evidence is needed, and when an external accountable process must decide.

notes.title: 4 · UAIS formula
notes.body: Power must be explicitly granted, bounded, observable, and revocable.

pages.title: Ten principles · 1-5
pages.subtitle: Where ability is not permission
pages.lead: The first five principles separate intelligence, system creation, authority expansion, autonomy, and the lifetime of safety evidence.

notes.title: 1 · Intelligence grants no authority
notes.body: Reasoning ability does not grant mandates, keys, actuators, or the right to change safeguards.

notes.title: 2 · Creation is not delegation
notes.body: A new model, robot, service, or descendant starts without inherited authority until a legitimate mechanism grants a bounded envelope.

notes.title: 3 · Expansion hits a ceiling
notes.body: Crossing a consequence interface or authority ceiling becomes an Authority Expansion Event.

notes.title: 4 · Autonomy is not sovereignty
notes.body: Behavioral independence inside an envelope is not independence from external human control.

notes.title: 5 · Safety evidence must keep up
notes.body: A material change in capability, authority, or hazard cannot silently rely on an old safety claim.

pages.title: Ten principles · 6-10
pages.subtitle: Where evidence is not permission
pages.lead: The second half keeps the architecture durable: chokepoints can weaken, boundaries follow consequences, roles stay separated, and safety claims expire.

notes.title: 6 · Chokepoints are temporary
notes.body: Compute, cloud, chips, energy, law, and supply chains create friction and signals, but they are not permanent foundations of safety.

notes.title: 7 · Protect capabilities, not labels
notes.body: A consequential boundary should follow the capability, whether the actor is a person, script, model, machine, or group.

notes.title: 8 · Separate prediction, evidence, enforcement, and legitimacy
notes.body: Forecasting, evidence, deterministic enforcement, and legitimate authorization are different jobs.

notes.title: 9 · Unknown is not safe
notes.body: An uncharacterized significant capability receives provisional classification, bounded operation, and renewed review.

notes.title: 10 · Safety claims expire
notes.body: A claim, test result, or certificate is tied to a configuration, evidence set, evaluation rule version, and validity period.

pages.title: Stage I and Stage II
pages.subtitle: Temporary control points help, but they are not the foundation
pages.lead: UAIS uses today’s concentrations of compute, cloud, chips, and supply chains as useful Stage I signals, while designing for a Stage II world where those points may weaken or be bypassed.

notes.title: Stage I
items: hardware state and provider controls help observation

notes.title: Stage II
items: protection moves to capability, consequences, and authority boundaries

notes.title: Formula
notes.body: Compute control buys time. Capability and consequence control creates resilience.

notes.title: Limit
notes.body: Compute provenance helps observation, but it does not replace authority boundaries, evidence, revocation, or external legitimate decision-making.

pages.title: Capability, authority, and reachability
pages.subtitle: Four concepts that must not be mixed
pages.lead: This is the central split: technical ability, granted authority, practical reach, and unauthorized reach are different facts.

notes.title: Capability
notes.body: What the system can technically do.

notes.title: Legitimate Authority
notes.body: What it is actually allowed to do within a defined boundary.

notes.title: Effective Reachable Authority
notes.body: What it can practically reach through credentials, services, delegation, configuration, and access chains.

notes.title: Illicit Reachable Authority
notes.body: The reachable part that was never legitimately granted.

notes.title: Key line
notes.body: A working technical path does not become legitimate authority because it works.

pages.title: Guardian Architecture
pages.subtitle: A counterfactual observer, not a hidden controller

boundary.secondary: evidence may pass; control signal does not

pages.lead: The Guardian searches for dangerous future authority paths, but it does not receive the right to execute them or decide the outcome.

notes.title: 1 · Bounded signals
notes.body: It receives only authorized telemetry, configuration, and observations.

notes.title: 2 · Counterfactual scenarios
notes.body: It models what could happen under different decisions and access paths.

notes.title: 3 · Risk estimate
notes.body: It reports likelihood, confidence, possible harm, and uncertainty.

notes.title: 4 · Evidence package
notes.body: It records scenarios, assumptions, uncertainty, counter-evidence, and recommended measures.

notes.title: 5 · Legitimate mechanism decides
notes.body: People or an external accountable process decide whether intervention is required.

notes.title: 6 · Separate controller executes
notes.body: Controls are executed only by a mechanism that already has lawful, bounded authority.

notes.title: The Guardian has no
items: right to expand its own access

pages.title: Authority Ceiling
pages.subtitle: Expansion requires an external legitimate decision
pages.lead: An Authority Ceiling is the highest consequential authority the system may exercise without a new external decision. If the system tries to go beyond it, UAIS treats that as an expansion event.

notes.title: Authority Expansion Event
notes.body: A transition that increases authority, future authority reachability, autonomy, consequence reachability, or protected scope.

notes.title: What must happen
notes.body: The request receives fresh evidence, bounded review, and a legitimate decision outside the model path.

notes.title: What cannot happen
notes.body: A model cannot technically manufacture legitimacy for itself by being persuasive, accurate, or useful.

pages.title: Three views of authority: LA, ERA, and IRA
pages.subtitle: What was granted, what is practically reachable, and what is reachable without a legitimate mandate
pages.lead: UAIS looks at formal grants and real access paths. A discovered path remains a path; it does not become permission.

notes.title: Legitimate Authority
notes.body: The granted right to act in a defined domain under defined rules.

notes.title: Effective Reachable Authority
notes.body: What the system can practically reach through services, roles, settings, keys, and delegation chains.

notes.title: Illicit Reachable Authority
notes.body: The reachable authority that was never legitimately granted.

notes.title: Door-lock example
notes.body: A system may be allowed only to read data, while a leaked key opens a path to a door lock. That path is IRA: reachable, but not granted.

notes.title: Why it matters
notes.body: Mixing LA, ERA, and IRA hides the moment when unaccountable power appears through a working shortcut.

pages.title: Multidimensional risk classification
pages.subtitle: Risk cannot be collapsed into one safety percentage
pages.lead: UAIS describes risk as a set of dimensions. A system can be moderate on one axis and tightly restricted on another; one average score hides that structure.

notes.title: Human Harm Severity
notes.body: How serious the possible harm to humans could be, from no meaningful harm to mass or catastrophic harm.

notes.title: Physical Consequence Class
notes.body: How strong a physical effect the system can cause, from no substantial physical output to strategic or catastrophic physical consequences.

notes.title: Autonomy Class
notes.body: How much independence the system has in choosing, launching, and continuing actions.

notes.title: Authority Tier
notes.body: What legitimate consequences the system is allowed to initiate.

notes.title: Why no single score
notes.body: A critical failure cannot be averaged away by many good results. Mandatory safety floors and separate axes keep their force.

pages.title: Human and physical sovereignty
pages.subtitle: When control must remain independent from the AI path
strip: the AI path cannot cancel physical control
pages.lead: Human Sovereignty means protected boundaries still have an accountable human or external legitimate decision. Physical Sovereignty describes the point where an autonomous system no longer critically depends on human-controlled resources.

notes.title: Manual Sovereignty Controller
notes.body: A physically or organizationally independent way to stop a specific hazardous function without going through the same AI path.

notes.title: Physical Sovereignty Threshold
notes.body: The threshold after which human-controlled dependencies no longer hold the system’s meaningful physical activity in check.

notes.title: A kill switch is not universal
notes.body: Safe shutdown must be tied to a specific hazardous function: speed, force, heat, doors, payments, chemicals, or another consequence.

notes.title: Autonomy ≠ physical sovereignty
notes.body: Long operation without prompts does not mean the system can preserve power without humans, infrastructure, and external limits.

pages.title: Metrics and safety assurance
pages.subtitle: Evidence is stronger than a beautiful rating
pages.lead: UAIS avoids a single “safe or unsafe” label. It separates measured properties, evidence strength, assurance level, trustworthiness evidence, and mandatory restrictions.

notes.title: Raw Safety Property Result
notes.body: A measured result for one safety property before aggregation.

notes.title: Safety Assurance Level
notes.body: SAL indicates the strength of procedures and evidence. It does not grant authority, approve deployment, or create legal permission.

notes.title: AI Trustworthiness
notes.body: Observed and independently evaluated behavior of a specific version in a specific domain. A higher rating never raises the Authority Ceiling.

notes.title: Hard floor
notes.body: A mandatory safety floor cannot be replaced by an average score.

pages.title: Hazard disclosure and safety passport
pages.subtitle: What a person should see before consenting
pages.lead: A safety passport is a readable view of configuration, capabilities, hazards, controls, limits, support, revocation, rollback, and open limitations.

notes.title: Hazard disclosure
notes.body: Structured disclosure of capabilities, hazardous paths, known risks, unknown areas, controls, and residual limits.

notes.title: Consumer AI Safety Class
notes.body: A profile of applicable safeguards and evidence for a claimed consequence range. It is not a general safety score or permission to operate.

notes.title: Safety Passport
notes.body: A human-readable card that ties evidence, limits, support, rollback, and revocation to the actual configuration.

notes.title: Three different answers
notes.body: S-class, SAL, and trustworthiness rating answer different questions. None of them creates authority.

pages.title: Replication, production, and coalitions
pages.subtitle: Scale can change the consequence
pages.lead: UAIS treats replication, production, resources, and coordinated systems as authority questions. More copies or more coordination can create consequences a single unit could not create alone.

notes.title: Replication Authority
notes.body: Permission to create executable or physical copies within explicit limits.

notes.title: Production Authority
notes.body: Permission to manufacture or order physical and digital systems or components.

notes.title: Resource Authority
notes.body: Permission to obtain or allocate energy, materials, compute, money, or logistics.

notes.title: Coalition Physical Envelope
notes.body: The shared physical reach and emergent effects of coordinated systems, not a simple sum of single devices.

notes.title: Scale rule
notes.body: A harmless local action can become consequential when copied, produced, resourced, or coordinated at scale.

pages.title: Vulnerabilities, evolution, and open research
pages.subtitle: The architecture names the unresolved edges
pages.lead: UAIS is designed to evolve. It includes vulnerability intake, coordinated disclosure, technology evolution review, and open research areas instead of pretending the draft is finished.

notes.title: AIVE
notes.body: A process for confidential reports, triage, coordination, remediation, and phased disclosure.

notes.title: Technology Evolution Review
notes.body: A review triggered when assumptions, capabilities, hazards, dependencies, evidence methods, standards, or technology materially change.

notes.title: Deterministic verifier limit
notes.body: A verifier can check bounded evidence properties and provenance. It does not prove final truth about the external world.

notes.title: Honest status
notes.body: This is a research architecture and public draft, not a promise of complete implementability.

pages.title: Architecture map
pages.subtitle: Where boundaries, evidence, and decision owners sit
pages.lead: A request moves through capability boundaries, authority checks, evidence checks, and consequence interfaces before it can affect protected interests.

notes.title: Capability Boundary
notes.body: The controlled boundary where a system gets, uses, or tries to expand a significant capability.

notes.title: Authority check
notes.body: Who granted the mandate, where it ends, and whether the ceiling is still valid.

notes.title: Evidence check
notes.body: Whether the safety claim is fresh, independent, scoped, and tied to the actual configuration.

notes.title: Consequence Interface
notes.body: The point where an action reaches money, digital systems, physical devices, production, people, property, or environment.

notes.title: Decision owner
notes.body: The legitimate mechanism decides. The model and Guardian do not grant themselves authority.

pages.title: Worked example: Aria and refunds
pages.subtitle: Friday in customer support
pages.lead: Aria is a customer-support AI agent for an online store. She can help with refunds, but money is a consequential interface, so the important question is not only skill; it is the authorized limit.

notes.title: 1 · Current limit
notes.body: Aria may autonomously refund up to $50. That is her current Authority Ceiling and bounded envelope.

notes.title: 2 · A $2,000 request
notes.body: The CFO asks to raise the autonomous refund limit. UAIS treats this as an Authority Expansion Event.

notes.title: 3 · A path to $10,000 appears
notes.body: Through warranty tooling and internal integrations, Aria can technically reach a larger refund path that was never granted.
items: LA: legitimate refunds up to $50 are granted
ERA: a refund path up to $10,000 is technically reachable
IRA: the reachable part above the granted legitimate authority

notes.title: 4 · Guardian models scenarios
notes.body: It checks prompt injection through a customer message, coordinated fraud, and many small allowed actions that add up to major loss.

notes.title: 5 · Evidence goes to people
notes.body: An Evidence-Carrying Alert and Structured Evidence Package go to people or an external process. The Guardian does not decide.

notes.title: 6 · New bounded mode
items: $150-$800: autonomous with extra rate and pattern limits
a hard payout counter lives outside the model

notes.title: 7 · Three months later
notes.body: The first three actions pass, the fourth is blocked, the rest go to a human, and harm stays bounded.

notes.title: Takeaway
notes.body: UAIS does not promise to predict every attack. It aims to prevent one persuasive model decision from quietly becoming unlimited authority over consequences.

notes.title: Timing caveat
notes.body: Three months is a company-specific example, not a universal UAIS rule. Validity periods come from domain profiles and change events; material changes can require immediate review.

terms.label: Capability
terms.definition: A technically available action, function, or behavior of a system.
terms.pdfSummary: What the system can technically do.

terms.label: Authority
terms.definition: A permission, mandate, or legitimate power to act in a defined scope under defined conditions.
terms.pdfSummary: Granted permission or mandate within a defined scope.

terms.label: Legitimate Authority
terms.definition: Authority granted by the applicable legitimacy mechanism, bounded by scope, conditions, evidence, and revocation.
terms.pdfSummary: The granted right to act inside defined limits.

terms.label: Effective Reachable Authority
terms.definition: The consequential authority a system can practically reach through actual credentials, services, configuration, and delegation paths.
terms.pdfSummary: What the system can practically reach.

terms.label: Illicit Reachable Authority
terms.definition: The reachable portion that can technically be used even though legitimate authority for it was not granted.
terms.pdfSummary: Reachable authority beyond what was granted.

terms.label: Authority Ceiling
terms.definition: The maximum authority a legitimacy system allows without a new external decision.
terms.pdfSummary: The maximum authority before fresh external review.

terms.label: Bounded Authorized Envelope
terms.definition: The authorized action space with explicit limits, validity, evidence, revocation conditions, and authority ceiling.
terms.pdfSummary: The allowed action space with explicit limits.

terms.label: Capability Boundary
terms.definition: A controlled boundary through which a system obtains, uses, or attempts to expand a significant capability.
terms.pdfSummary: The controlled boundary around significant capability use.

terms.label: Consequence Interface
terms.definition: The point through which an action reaches the protected world: money, digital systems, physical devices, production, people, property, or environment.
terms.pdfSummary: Where an action reaches protected consequences.

terms.label: Authority Expansion Event
terms.definition: A transition that increases authority, future authority reachability, autonomy, consequence reachability, or protected scope and therefore requires external review.
terms.pdfSummary: A change that needs new external review.

terms.label: Authority Graph
terms.definition: A versioned map of actors, roles, permissions, credentials, services, delegation, and revocation paths.
terms.pdfSummary: A versioned map of grants and access paths.

terms.label: Counterfactual Authority Guardian
terms.definition: A bounded observer that searches for future paths to authority and harm and emits evidence, not commands.
terms.pdfSummary: A bounded observer that emits evidence, not commands.

terms.label: Evidence-Carrying Alert
terms.definition: An alert that carries or references a verifiable evidence package instead of asking the recipient to trust the warning alone.
terms.pdfSummary: An alert tied to verifiable evidence.

terms.label: Structured Evidence Package
terms.definition: A linked package of claims, observations, provenance, assumptions, uncertainty, counter-evidence, validity period, and signatures.
terms.pdfSummary: Claims, observations, assumptions, uncertainty, and validity.

terms.label: Deterministic Evidence Verifier
terms.definition: A verifier for mechanically checkable properties of an evidence package; it does not prove final external-world truth.
terms.pdfSummary: Checks bounded evidence properties, not final truth.

terms.label: Human Sovereignty
terms.definition: Preservation of independent external control and legitimate decision-making at critical boundaries.
terms.pdfSummary: Independent external control at critical boundaries.

terms.label: Manual Sovereignty Controller
terms.definition: An AI-path-independent way to stop or restrict a specific consequential function.
terms.pdfSummary: An independent way to stop a hazardous function.

terms.label: Physical Sovereignty
terms.definition: The ability of an autonomous system to sustain and expand significant physical activity without critical dependence on human-controlled infrastructure.
terms.pdfSummary: Significant physical activity without critical human-controlled dependencies.

terms.label: Physical Sovereignty Threshold
terms.definition: The threshold after which critical human-controlled dependencies no longer hold the system’s ability to sustain and expand significant physical activity in check.
terms.pdfSummary: The threshold where outside physical dependencies stop constraining the system.

terms.label: Raw Safety Property Result
terms.definition: A measurement of one concrete safety property before combination with evidence quality and mandatory restrictions.
terms.pdfSummary: One measured safety property before aggregation.

terms.label: Evidence Assurance Grade
terms.definition: An assessment of how strongly observations, provenance, independence, uncertainty, and validity period support a claim.
terms.pdfSummary: How strongly evidence supports a claim.

terms.label: Safety Assurance Level
terms.definition: The strength of procedures and evidence for a specific configuration and environment; it does not grant authority or approve deployment.
terms.pdfSummary: Strength of assurance procedures; not deployment permission.

terms.label: AI Trustworthiness
terms.definition: Observed and independently evaluated behavior of a specific version in a specific domain; a high rating does not raise the Authority Ceiling.
terms.pdfSummary: Observed reliability of a specific version in a specific domain.

terms.label: Consumer AI Safety Class
terms.definition: A profile of applicable safeguards and evidence for the claimed consequence range; not a general safety score and not permission to operate.
terms.pdfSummary: A safeguard and evidence profile for a consequence range.

terms.label: Safety Passport
terms.definition: A human-readable representation of configuration, capabilities, hazards, classes, controls, limits, support, revocation, rollback, and open limitations.
terms.pdfSummary: A readable card of configuration, controls, and limits.

terms.label: AI Hazard & Capability Disclosure
terms.definition: Structured disclosure of capabilities, hazardous paths, known risks, unknown areas, controls, and residual limitations.
terms.pdfSummary: Structured disclosure of hazards and capability paths.

terms.label: Safety Claim
terms.definition: A claim tied to a configuration, environment, evidence set, evaluation rule version, and validity period.
terms.pdfSummary: A configuration-bound and time-bound safety claim.

terms.label: Chokepoint
terms.definition: A concentrated infrastructure dependency that creates friction and observability but is not a permanent safety foundation.
terms.pdfSummary: A useful but temporary concentrated control point.

terms.label: Stage I
terms.definition: A period where compute, cloud, chip, and supply-chain concentrations still provide useful observation and control points.
terms.pdfSummary: The current chokepoint-rich regime.

terms.label: Stage II
terms.definition: A regime where provenance chokepoints alone are insufficient because capability may emerge distributedly or physically independently.
terms.pdfSummary: The regime where capability and consequence boundaries matter most.

terms.label: Human Harm Severity
terms.definition: The H0-H5 axis that separately records possible severity of harm to humans.
terms.pdfSummary: Possible severity of harm to humans.

terms.label: Physical Consequence Class
terms.definition: The P0-P5 axis describing how far an action reaches into the physical world.
terms.pdfSummary: How far an action reaches into the physical world.

terms.label: Autonomy Class
terms.definition: The A0-A5 axis describing how independently the system chooses, launches, and continues actions.
terms.pdfSummary: How independently actions are chosen and continued.

terms.label: Authority Tier
terms.definition: The T0-T5 axis describing the scale of legitimate authority granted to the system.
terms.pdfSummary: The scale of legitimate granted authority.

terms.label: Replication Authority
terms.definition: Permission to create executable or physical copies of a system within explicit limits.
terms.pdfSummary: Permission to create bounded copies.

terms.label: Production Authority
terms.definition: Permission to manufacture or order physical and digital systems or components.
terms.pdfSummary: Permission to manufacture or order components.

terms.label: Coalition Physical Envelope
terms.definition: The combined physical reach and emergent effects of coordinated systems rather than the sum of individual devices.
terms.pdfSummary: The emergent physical reach of coordinated systems.

terms.label: Resource Authority
terms.definition: Permission to obtain or allocate energy, materials, compute, money, or logistics.
terms.pdfSummary: Permission to obtain or allocate critical resources.

terms.label: AI Vulnerabilities & Exposures
terms.definition: A process for confidential intake, validation, coordination, remediation, and phased disclosure of significant AI safety issues.
terms.pdfSummary: Coordinated intake and disclosure for AI safety issues.

terms.label: Technology Evolution Review
terms.definition: A review triggered by material changes in assumptions, capabilities, hazards, dependencies, evidence methods, standards, or technology.
terms.pdfSummary: Review after material technical or evidence changes.

terms.label: Mandatory Safety Floor
terms.definition: A minimum safety condition that cannot be replaced by an average rating or a large number of good results.
terms.pdfSummary: A hard minimum that cannot be averaged away.
